translations.title: Water and wastewater CMMS advisory: structure upstream planning to secure the roadmap
translations.seoTitle: Water and wastewater CMMS advisory: structure upstream planning to secure the roadmap
translations.seoDescription: In CMMS projects for water, wastewater or municipal technical services, the upstream phase is critical to success. OLING prioritises rigorous scoping, clear requirements and documented governance to avoid common pitfalls. This methodology secures every stage, distinguishes business needs from software selection and turns initial uncertainty into a shared roadmap.

translations.heroIntro: Before approaching a CMMS vendor or integrator, organisations must assess the assets to be maintained, maintenance processes, data to be migrated, mobile use cases and interfaces with the wider IT landscape. In water and wastewater operations, GIS, equipment master data and field constraints must be addressed from the scoping stage.
translations.heroSideHtml:
Upstream CMMS scoping starts in the field

Before approaching a CMMS vendor or integrator, organisations must assess the assets to be maintained, maintenance processes, data to be migrated, mobile use cases and interfaces with the wider IT landscape. In water and wastewater operations, GIS, equipment master data and field constraints must be addressed from the scoping stage.

Scoping must examine how teams prepare, carry out and close maintenance tasks. It must also distinguish between business processes, field operations, data, software configuration and interfaces with the wider information system.

Assets, equipment and technical hierarchy

The technical hierarchy determines the quality of the entire CMMS. It must make it possible to find equipment, track its history, schedule maintenance and produce actionable reports. A hierarchy that is too detailed becomes impossible to maintain, while one that is too limited prevents effective analysis of incidents and costs.

Before going to tender, the required levels must therefore be defined: site, facility, area, equipment, sub-equipment, meter, device or critical component. The right level depends on the intended uses, including preventive maintenance, on-call support, regulatory monitoring, inventory, costs, availability and traceability.

Master data and data quality

The master data to be scoped includes equipment, locations, technical categories, maintenance procedures, parts, suppliers, contracts, teams, authorisations and maintenance priorities. This data must be assessed before import, as late migration often delays configuration, acceptance testing and field deployment.

CMMS data migration must be prepared before final configuration. Equipment, locations, technical hierarchies, maintenance histories, inventory and maintenance procedures must be assessed before import. The scoping phase must specify what will be migrated, cleansed, discarded or rebuilt.

Preventive and corrective maintenance, mobility and inventory

Preventive maintenance requires clear procedures, justified frequencies and well-defined responsibilities. Corrective maintenance requires straightforward request classification, clear priorities and a closure process that produces actionable information. Field mobility must be designed around real operating conditions: areas without network coverage, rapid data entry, attachments, photos, signatures and geolocation where useful and authorised.

Inventory processes must be scoped with maintenance and finance teams, covering critical parts, thresholds, issues, returns, valuation, stocktaking and potential links with procurement. A theoretical inventory accuracy target should not be promised without confirming the organisation’s actual ability to keep the data current.

Interfaces to clarify before going to tender

A CMMS may need to exchange data with a GIS, ERP, customer information system, supervisory control system, request portal, finance solution or HR master data system. Each interface must be described in terms of its purpose, exchanged data, frequency, flow direction, owner and expected controls.

GIS is often central to water and wastewater operations, but it does not replace the maintenance hierarchy. Organisations must decide which system is the authoritative source for each type of data and how discrepancies will be detected.

Tendering, acceptance testing and deployment

The tender documentation must reflect priority use cases without locking the project into a predetermined solution. Selection criteria must cover functional fit, data migration, mobility, interfaces, field usability, administration capabilities and implementation commitments.

Acceptance testing must not focus solely on screens. It must replay business scenarios: creating a request, converting it into a maintenance task, assignment, field data entry, issuing inventory, closure, verification, reporting and correcting an error. Deployment must include training, go-live support, final data migration and data governance rules.

For support with requirements scoping, tendering, data migration and acceptance testing, see our CMMS advisory services. When the CMMS forms part of a broader programme, scoping may also be covered by our IT project advisory and transformation management services.

translations.title: CRM: structuring cybersecurity and governing without unnecessary exposure
translations.seoTitle: CRM: structuring cybersecurity and governing without unnecessary exposure
translations.seoDescription: When implementing a custom CRM, cybersecurity cannot be reduced to a checklist or a promise of absolute protection. OLING offers a structured, pragmatic approach focused on prioritising key issues, producing streamlined deliverables and managing communications to ensure credible governance without unnecessary exposure.
translations.heroTitle: Custom CRM: structuring cybersecurity and governing without illusion or unnecessary exposure
translations.heroIntro: When implementing a custom CRM, cybersecurity cannot be reduced to a checklist or a promise of absolute protection. OLING offers a structured, pragmatic approach focused on prioritising key issues, producing streamlined deliverables and managing communications to ensure credible governance without unnecessary exposure.
translations.heroSideHtml:
Custom CRM: cybersecurity as a matter of governance and methodology

Redesigning or deploying a custom CRM in an industrial or B2B environment presents IT departments and business teams with a major challenge: integrating cybersecurity without relying on generic solutions or reassuring claims. Digital transformation expands the attack surface; governance must therefore make clear-sighted decisions that balance operational efficiency, compliance and controlled communication.

Prioritise without losing focus: the pitfalls of multiple workstreams

In practice, the proliferation of security initiatives—audits, tools, awareness and compliance—frequently leads to an accumulation of tasks that are rarely prioritised. This lack of prioritisation creates two major risks:

  • An action plan that is too broad to govern effectively.
  • Communication that, if poorly calibrated, unnecessarily exposes sensitive matters or creates the impression of complete security.

OLING structures its approach around an initial scoping phase: accurately identifying the priorities and constraints of the specific context, then building a realistic roadmap that is suitable for sharing and easy for leadership to understand. This approach prevents resources from being spread too thinly and protects the confidentiality of sensitive information.

Structuring action: three steps towards a credible cybersecurity plan

The success of a custom CRM project depends on formalising a progressive, tailored cybersecurity plan. OLING favours a clear sequence:

  • Identifying priorities and constraints: mapping key issues without ever disclosing details of vulnerabilities or incidents.
  • Structuring the work plan: sequencing actions, documenting decisions and establishing regular reviews, without ever promising absolute security.
  • Formalising deliverables: a summary of priorities, an action plan and a governance framework tailored to the context and approved by leadership.

This approach establishes a culture of continuous improvement while avoiding any confusion between awareness and a promise of comprehensive protection.

Managing communication: vigilance and editorial discipline

In a context where the temptation to use reassuring or highly technical language is strong, OLING recommends strict discipline:

  • Never disclose sensitive information, even in internal discussions or governance materials.
  • Do not confuse awareness with assurance: education should support decision-making, not conceal the limitations of the measures in place.
  • Maintain a restricted scope of communication: governance gains credibility by favouring restraint over technical exhaustiveness.

OLING deliverables are intentionally streamlined and focused on areas for improvement and key decisions. They avoid excessive technical detail and unrealistic promises.

Governing cybersecurity over the long term

The value of a cybersecurity plan is not measured by the length of a checklist, but by governance’s ability to uphold its priorities, make decisions and maintain oversight over time. OLING establishes focused routines: progress reviews, anonymised summaries and approval of key decisions. A leadership-friendly priority dashboard distinguishes between completed, ongoing and planned matters without ever crossing the line into disclosing sensitive information.

Conclusion: establish a credible methodology, not an illusion of protection

Structuring cybersecurity for a custom CRM means rejecting headline-grabbing claims and promises of complete protection. OLING prioritises methodological clarity, incremental progress and human approval. A credible, shareable framework compatible with anonymisation helps secure the project without ever overpromising.

translations.title: BCP/DRP: structure continuity, avoid illusions
translations.seoDescription: Formalising a business continuity plan (BCP) or disaster recovery plan (DRP) only adds value if the process highlights genuine business priorities and clarifies critical dependencies. OLING offers a pragmatic, progressive and governed approach focused on actionable deliverables and realistic risk management, far removed from unrealistic promises or plans disconnected from operational realities.
translations.heroIntro: Formalising a business continuity plan (BCP) or disaster recovery plan (DRP) only adds value if the process highlights genuine business priorities and clarifies critical dependencies. OLING offers a pragmatic, progressive and governed approach focused on actionable deliverables and realistic risk management, far removed from unrealistic promises or plans disconnected from operational realities.
translations.heroSideHtml:
Clarifying continuity: first and foremost, a governance issue

In most organisations, drafting a Business Continuity Plan (BCP) or Disaster Recovery Plan (DRP) is often seen as a formality. Yet the real challenge lies neither in technology nor in documentary compliance, but in the ability to establish a framework that highlights priorities and enables genuinely manageable trade-offs.

The limitations of plans disconnected from the business

  • Plans that are difficult to put into action: generic documents drafted for compliance purposes, but with little relevance to real-life situations.
  • Poorly understood critical dependencies: incomplete maps that leave major blind spots across the value chain.
  • Unrealistic promises: guaranteeing recovery under all circumstances is more an illusion than effective operational control.

OLING’s approach: define the scope, prioritise and formalise without overpromising

OLING favours a structured, progressive approach tailored to the organisation’s actual level of maturity. The aim is not to accumulate pages, but to make decisions clear and usable by business teams and the IT department:

  • Scoping critical requirements: clearly identify vital functions and the tipping points on which continuity depends.
  • Prioritising scenarios and dependencies: rank risks and clarify interdependencies without overloading the plan with sensitive or technical information.
  • Progressive work plan: build a realistic, adaptable roadmap that reflects available resources and constraints.

This method is designed to support effective management rather than compliance with a fixed template (source: Practice pca-et-pra).

Useful deliverables designed to last

  • Summary of critical requirements: a clear document that can be used by both business and IT teams, establishing the fundamentals without exposing sensitive details.
  • Business continuity or disaster recovery plan: concise, actionable and aligned with explicit priorities, with a design that makes updates straightforward.
  • Prioritisation framework: a matrix documenting assumptions, trade-offs and key dependencies to support evolving governance.

These deliverables are designed to be reused, updated regularly and shared without creating unnecessary risk (source: Practice pca-et-pra).

What OLING rejects: empty promises and unnecessary exposure

  • Avoid exposing sensitive details: every plan should remain at the governance level without creating vulnerabilities around critical operations.
  • No absolute guarantees: OLING clarifies the conditions and limitations of continuity without ever promising the impossible.
  • Maintain alignment between governance and the business: a plan’s value depends on the relevant stakeholders’ ability to understand, manage and update it.

In summary: manage continuity, not appearances

A credible BCP or DRP is judged not by the thickness of the document, but by the clarity of its trade-offs and how easily it can be activated in a real-life situation. For IT departments, business leaders and project managers, a clear prioritisation framework, an up-to-date plan and an actionable summary remain the best safeguards against the unexpected. OLING structures this framework without ever promising total control, while ensuring that its foundations remain sound.

translations.title: Territorial data portal: structure the roadmap, avoid fragmentation and establish sustainable governance
translations.seoTitle: Territorial data portal: structure the roadmap, avoid fragmentation and establish sustainable governance
translations.seoDescription: Designing a territorial data portal is not merely a technical challenge. Without robust governance, clear priorities and ongoing oversight, efforts can become diluted and dependencies excessive. Through its outsourced CIO practice, OLING helps turn this type of initiative into a strategic enabler by sequencing workstreams, formalising decisions and safeguarding long-term progress.
translations.heroTitle: Territorial data portal: structure the roadmap, avoid fragmentation and establish sustainable governance
translations.heroIntro: Designing a territorial data portal is not merely a technical challenge. Without robust governance, clear priorities and ongoing oversight, efforts can become diluted and dependencies excessive. Through its outsourced CIO practice, OLING helps turn this type of initiative into a strategic enabler by sequencing workstreams, formalising decisions and safeguarding long-term progress.
translations.heroSideHtml:
Territorial data portal: move beyond technology and establish robust governance

Implementing a data portal for a regional organisation—incorporating GIS connectors, business data repositories, and public and professional access—can never be reduced to selecting tools. The central challenge is to establish appropriate governance capable of channelling collective energy towards shared, documented priorities.

Concurrent workstreams: an underestimated risk

Initial enthusiasm often leads to several workstreams being launched at once: GIS data integration, platform development, and tailored access for different audiences. Without precise oversight, this concurrency quickly results in:

  • Fragmented efforts and dispersed resources;
  • Essential decisions being postponed or bypassed;
  • Dependence on a small number of key individuals, making the project vulnerable;
  • Unspoken expectations remaining unaddressed and generating tensions later.

OLING outsourced CIO services: establishing a progressive governance framework

OLING draws on its outsourced CIO practice to create a framework in which every stage of the project is supported by:

  • A precise IT assessment: mapping data flows and identifying dependencies and major pain points;
  • Formal prioritisation of issues and risks, distinguishing urgent matters from strategic priorities;
  • Ongoing oversight, ensuring clear visibility of progress and traceable decision-making.

This support prevents tunnel vision and allows the added value of each phase to be validated, without promising rapid transformation or positioning itself as a universal replacement for an internal IT department.

Concrete deliverables and organisational vigilance

The robustness of an outsourced CIO approach is reflected in the quality of its deliverables:

  • IT roadmap: clearly defined milestones, dependencies and areas of uncertainty;
  • Governance framework: clarified roles, defined oversight arrangements and decision-making bodies;
  • Summary of priorities: a basis for dialogue between business teams, IT and technical partners.

Two areas of concern are systematically monitored:

  • Avoid basing governance on a small number of pivotal individuals, thereby preventing structural vulnerabilities;
  • Formalise expectations, including implicit ones, to prevent misunderstandings and obstacles along the way.

Step-by-step progress: build on achievements and adapt without disruption

OLING’s approach favours short cycles in which every advance is reviewed and adjusted collaboratively. This pace:

  • Helps consolidate achievements;
  • Allows the roadmap to be redirected without losing coherence;
  • Establishes a culture of governance that is essential to the portal’s long-term sustainability beyond its launch.

Conclusion: anchor the portal’s value in IT governance

A territorial data portal is neither a straightforward technical integration project nor an institutional showcase. Its success depends on the ability to structure decisions, document priorities and establish governance that stands the test of time. OLING’s outsourced CIO practice provides this methodical, progressive framework, ensuring a clear roadmap and lasting value creation.

This approach gives every stakeholder—business teams, IT and partners—a clear place within the governance structure, free from the illusion of universal solutions and hidden dependencies.

translations.title: QHSE, performance and internal control: building engagement in a public port organisation
translations.seoTitle: QHSE, performance and internal control: building engagement in a public port organisation
translations.seoDescription: In large public port organisations, QHSE and performance management are not about piling up controls or claiming full compliance. OLING provides an internal control framework that clarifies roles, focuses on priority control points and formalises approval workflows suited to operational realities. This progressive approach, centred on concrete deliverables, helps overcome internal inertia and build lasting engagement.
translations.heroTitle: QHSE, performance and internal control: building engagement in a public port organisation
translations.heroIntro: In large public port organisations, QHSE and performance management are not about piling up controls or claiming full compliance. OLING provides an internal control framework that clarifies roles, focuses on priority control points and formalises approval workflows suited to operational realities. This progressive approach, centred on concrete deliverables, helps overcome internal inertia and build lasting engagement.
translations.heroSideHtml:
Creating structure without illusions: moving beyond QHSE claims to establish credible governance

In a public port environment, performance and business process management cannot be reduced to either regulatory compliance or a succession of controls. QHSE (Quality, Health, Safety and Environment) initiatives often face internal obstacles: fragmented practices, difficulty connecting controls with actual operations and unclear approval responsibilities. The challenge is to establish a clear, sustainable framework that goes beyond simply preventing non-compliance to support collective, measurable progress.

Clarify, prioritise and formalise: OLING’s approach to internal control

OLING structures internal control around three key drivers:

  • Identify priority control points: The aim is not to multiply checks, but to select those that genuinely support performance and risk management.
  • Clarify roles and approvals: Everyone involved must understand their responsibilities, the approval workflows and how decisions are documented and shared.
  • Structure the improvement roadmap: Progress is achieved over time through concrete, shareable deliverables that can adapt as projects and teams evolve.

Key considerations: avoid excessive controls and encourage ownership

Common pitfalls include accumulating controls disconnected from operational realities and pursuing an illusion of exhaustive coverage. OLING highlights two major risks:

  • Accumulation without ownership: Too many checkpoints undermine momentum and dilute responsibility.
  • The pursuit of exhaustive coverage: Aiming for complete coverage leads to a loss of focus and reduced effectiveness. It is better to target relevant risks and embed controls in day-to-day business practices.

Deliverables that embed progress and make it visible

The value of an internal control approach is measured by the clarity and long-term usefulness of its deliverables. OLING prioritises:

  • A control map: To show key control points, their owners and approval workflows. Shared with the relevant committee, this map provides tangible evidence of progress and highlights areas that need to be strengthened.
  • A summary of roles and responsibilities: To clarify who does what, eliminate grey areas and facilitate collective ownership.
  • An action plan: To organise progress, manage adoption and adjust the framework over time.

Building engagement: methods and evidence rather than rhetoric

Engagement cannot be secured through instructions or by multiplying tools. It is built by making the purpose of controls clear, involving stakeholders as soon as roles are formalised and adapting the roadmap to operational realities. In the port sector, demonstrating progress through evolving deliverables, such as control maps and shared summaries, helps turn QHSE into a driver of engagement and efficiency, even when facing initial inertia.

Conclusion: establishing an operational, sustainable and credible framework

Strengthening QHSE and business process management in a public port organisation is not about appearances or promises of full compliance. Structuring internal control means accepting step-by-step progress, prioritising clarity over exhaustive coverage and building on deliverables that sustain collective momentum. It also means establishing governance in which everyone can clearly assess how their actions affect overall performance.

Key takeaway: a control map shared with the relevant committee provides tangible evidence of progress and a practical basis for managing adjustments and building lasting trust.
